title: Talent May Be Portable But Success Is Not
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article pushes back on the popular idea that skilled remote-era talent can move seamlessly between organizations, arguing that much of what makes someone successful is embedded in the specific culture, relationships, and institutional knowledge of their current workplace. It walks through several non-portable advantages — internal networks, familiarity with processes and unwritten rules, and established trust — that new hires must rebuild from scratch, often while facing quiet suspicion from new peers. Citing research that most top performers fail to replicate their prior success after switching organizations, the piece urges both leaders and employees to weigh what is genuinely transferable before assuming a move will go smoothly.
points: Remote work has fueled the perception that top talent is highly portable across organizations.
Much of what drives an individual's success is tied to organization-specific culture, relationships, and processes, not to the person alone.
New hires often face quiet suspicion from peers competing for the same resources, complicating a fast start.
Learning an organization's unwritten rules and internal navigation takes significant time performance typically suffers in the meantime.
Research cited in the piece suggests most top performers fail to reach their prior level of success after changing organizations.
quotes: In a world of fleeting organizational loyalty and remote work, the realization of how portable talent is has become top of mind for many leaders.
The idea that highly skilled team members can make a fast transition and apply their experience and knowledge in a new organization, however, is drastically overstated.
Worse yet, new colleagues are often looked at suspiciously once they land in an unfamiliar workplace.
Every organization has its secret doors and magic words that make life easier once you know them.
Research suggests that most top performers fail to reach the same level of success they enjoyed in the organization they recently left.
